Hearing Issues.education:
What are Hearing Issues?
Hearing loss is a partial or total inability to hear sounds in one or both ears. It can range from mild to profound and may be caused by aging, noise exposure, infections, genetics, or other medical conditions. Hearing loss can significantly affect communication, safety, and quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Difficulty hearing conversations, especially in noisy environments
•Frequently asking others to repeat themselves
•Turning up the volume on TV, radio, or phone
•Difficulty hearing on the telephone
•Muffled hearing
•Ringing, buzzing, or hissing in the ears (tinnitus)
•Difficulty understanding speech, especially high-pitched voices
•Withdrawal from social situations due to difficulty hearing
•Feeling that others are mumbling

Risk Factors:
•Aging (presbycusis)
•Chronic exposure to loud noises
•Family history of hearing loss
•Certain medications (ototoxic drugs)
•Chronic ear infections
•Head trauma
•Diabetes and cardiovascular disease
•Smoking

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Use prescribed hearing aids consistently and maintain them properly.
•Attend regular audiology appointments for hearing evaluations and hearing aid adjustments.
•Protect hearing by avoiding loud noise exposure and using ear protection.
•Face the speaker and maintain eye contact during conversations.
•Reduce background noise when possible.
•Use assistive listening devices, captioning, or visual alerts as needed.
•Keep ears clean but avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.
•Report sudden hearing loss, ear pain, or drainage immediately.
•Keep all scheduled audiology and ENT appointments.

Cancer.education:
What is Cancer?
Cancer is a group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells. If the spread is not controlled, it can result in death. Cancer can develop in almost any organ or tissue in the body. Treatment depends on the type, location, and stage of cancer.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Unexplained weight loss
•Fatigue that does not improve with rest
•Pain that does not go away
•Skin changes (darkening, yellowing, redness, sores that do not heal)
•Changes in bowel or bladder habits
•Persistent cough or trouble breathing
•Difficulty swallowing
•Unusual bleeding or discharge
•Lumps or thickening in the body
•Fever or night sweats
•Changes in moles or skin spots

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Family history of cancer
•Tobacco use
•Excessive alcohol consumption
•Obesity
•Excessive sun exposure
•Exposure to radiation or certain chemicals
•Certain infections (HPV, hepatitis)
•Chronic inflammation
•Immunosuppression
•Sedentary lifestyle
•Poor diet

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the treatment plan prescribed by the oncology team.
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Attend all scheduled chemotherapy, radiation, or immunotherapy sessions.
•Report side effects from treatment to the oncology team.
•Maintain adequate nutrition and hydration.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Manage pain with the healthcare provider's guidance.
•Attend follow-up appointments for monitoring and surveillance.
•Seek emotional and psychological support.
•Complete recommended cancer screenings for early detection.
•Address advance care planning.

Hx of Renal Cancer.education:
What is Renal Cancer (Kidney Cancer)?
Renal cancer, or kidney cancer, begins in the kidneys. The most common type in adults is renal cell carcinoma. For individuals with a history of renal cancer, ongoing surveillance and management of risk factors are important to monitor for recurrence and maintain overall kidney health.

Signs and Symptoms (of recurrence or ongoing issues):
•Blood in the urine (hematuria)
•Persistent pain in the side, back, or abdomen
•A lump or mass in the side or abdomen
•Unexplained weight loss
•Fatigue
•Fever not caused by infection
•Loss of appetite
•Bone pain (if metastatic)
•Swelling of the ankles or legs

Risk Factors:
•Smoking
•Obesity
•High blood pressure
•Family history of kidney cancer
•Certain genetic conditions (Von Hippel-Lindau disease)
•Long-term dialysis
•Exposure to certain chemicals
•Older age
•Male sex

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the surveillance schedule recommended by the oncologist (imaging, labs).
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Monitor remaining kidney function with regular lab work.
•Maintain blood pressure within the recommended range.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Stop smoking.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Report new or recurring symptoms immediately.
•Keep all scheduled oncology, urology, nephrology, and PCP appointments.

Laryngeal Cancer.education:
What is Laryngeal Cancer?
Laryngeal cancer is cancer that forms in the tissues of the larynx (voice box). The larynx is located in the throat and plays a role in breathing, swallowing, and speaking. Most laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Persistent hoarseness or voice changes
•Sore throat that does not improve
•Difficulty or pain when swallowing
•Ear pain
•A lump or mass in the neck
•Persistent cough
•Difficulty breathing or noisy breathing (stridor)
•Unintended weight loss
•Bad breath

Risk Factors:
•Tobacco use (strongest risk factor)
•Heavy alcohol use
•Combined tobacco and alcohol use (greatly increases risk)
•HPV infection
•Older age
•Male sex
•Poor nutrition
•Exposure to certain workplace chemicals (asbestos, paint fumes)
•GERD

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the treatment plan from the oncology team (surgery, radiation, chemotherapy).
•Take prescribed medications as directed.
•Attend speech therapy if voice changes occur after treatment.
•Follow swallowing therapy recommendations.
•Maintain adequate nutrition, using modified diets or feeding tubes if needed.
•Stop smoking and avoid alcohol.
•Attend all follow-up appointments for surveillance.
•Report new or recurring symptoms promptly.
•Seek emotional and psychological support.

References:

Skin Cancer.education:
What is Skin Cancer?
Skin cancer is the abnormal growth of skin cells, most often developing on skin exposed to the sun. The three main types are basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma. Early detection and treatment significantly improve outcomes.

Signs and Symptoms:
•A new growth, spot, or bump that is getting larger
•A sore that does not heal within a few weeks
•A spot or sore that itches, hurts, scabs, crusts, or bleeds
•A mole that changes in size, shape, color, or texture
•A mole with irregular borders, uneven color, or asymmetry
•A shiny, waxy, or pearly bump
•A flat, flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion
•A firm, red nodule

ABCDE Rule for Melanoma:
•A – Asymmetry: one half does not match the other
•B – Border: edges are irregular or blurred
•C – Color: color is uneven or includes shades of brown, black, pink, red, white, or blue
•D – Diameter: larger than 6 mm (size of a pencil eraser)
•E – Evolving: the spot is changing in size, shape, or color

Risk Factors:
•Excessive UV exposure (sun, tanning beds)
•History of sunburns, especially blistering sunburns
•Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
•Many moles or atypical moles
•Family history of skin cancer
•Personal history of skin cancer
•Weakened immune system
•Older age
•Exposure to certain chemicals

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the dermatologist's and oncologist's treatment plan.
•Perform monthly skin self-examinations.
•Protect skin from UV exposure (sunscreen SPF 30+, protective clothing, shade).
•Avoid tanning beds.
•Attend regular dermatology appointments for skin checks.
•Report any new, changing, or suspicious skin lesions promptly.
•Keep all follow-up appointments for surveillance.

HIV/AIDS.education:
What is HIV/AIDS?
HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that attacks the body's immune system, specifically the CD4 cells (T cells). If not treated, HIV can lead to AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome), the late stage of HIV infection when the immune system is severely damaged. With proper treatment (antiretroviral therapy), people with HIV can live long, healthy lives and prevent transmission.

Signs and Symptoms:
Early HIV infection:
•Flu-like symptoms 2-4 weeks after infection (fever, chills, rash, night sweats, muscle aches, sore throat, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, mouth ulcers)
•Some people may have no symptoms for years

Progressive HIV/AIDS:
•Rapid weight loss
•Recurring fever or night sweats
•Extreme fatigue
•Prolonged swelling of lymph nodes
•Chronic diarrhea
•Sores of the mouth, anus, or genitals
•Pneumonia
•Memory loss and neurological disorders
•Skin rashes or blotches
•Opportunistic infections

Risk Factors:
•Unprotected sexual contact
•Sharing needles or syringes
•Occupational exposure to infected blood
•Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding
•Blood transfusion (rare in the US due to screening)
•Having other sexually transmitted infections

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take antiretroviral therapy (ART) exactly as prescribed, every day, without missing doses.
•Do not stop or change ART without consulting the infectious disease specialist.
•Complete all recommended laboratory tests (viral load, CD4 count, resistance testing).
•Attend all scheduled infectious disease and PCP appointments.
•Practice safer sex and use condoms.
•Do not share needles.
•Receive recommended vaccinations.
•Maintain a healthy diet and stay physically active.
•Avoid smoking and limit alcohol.
•Report new symptoms, side effects, or signs of infection promptly.
•Seek mental health support as needed.
•Disclose HIV status to healthcare providers and sexual partners.

Pulmonary Hypertension.education:
What is Pulmonary Hypertension?
Pulmonary hypertension is a condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs is higher than normal. This makes the heart work harder to pump blood through the lungs, which can damage the heart over time. Pulmonary hypertension can develop on its own or be caused by another disease or condition.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with physical activity
•Fatigue or weakness
•Dizziness or fainting (syncope)
•Chest pain or pressure
•Swelling (edema) of the ankles, legs, or abdomen
•Rapid heartbeat or palpitations
•Bluish color of the lips or skin (cyanosis)
•Decreased exercise tolerance

Risk Factors:
•Left-sided heart disease such as heart failure or valve disease
•Chronic lung diseases such as COPD, emphysema, or pulmonary fibrosis
•Sleep apnea
•Blood clots in the lungs (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension)
•Connective tissue diseases such as scleroderma or lupus
•Congenital heart defects
•Family history of pulmonary hypertension
•Living at high altitudes
•Certain medications or illegal drug use
•HIV infection
•Liver disease (portal hypertension)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed, including vasodilators, endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, or other pulmonary hypertension-specific therapies.
•Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
•Follow sodium and fluid restrictions as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider; participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
•Weigh yourself daily and report sudden weight gain.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
•Avoid pregnancy if advised by the healthcare provider, as it can be life-threatening with pulmonary hypertension.
•Avoid high altitudes unless discussed with the healthcare provider.
•Keep all scheduled cardiology, pulmonology, and PCP appointments.
•Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

Bronchiectasis.education:
What is Bronchiectasis?
Bronchiectasis is a chronic condition in which the bronchial tubes (airways) of the lungs become permanently widened, damaged, and thickened. This damage allows mucus to build up, making the lungs more vulnerable to infection. Bronchiectasis can result from a variety of conditions that damage the airways.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Chronic cough that produces large amounts of mucus (sputum) daily
•Mucus that may be thick, discolored, or foul-smelling
•Shortness of breath
•Wheezing
•Recurrent respiratory infections
•Coughing up blood (hemoptysis)
•Chest pain
•Fatigue
•Clubbing of the fingertips (in advanced cases)

Risk Factors:
•History of severe or recurrent lung infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis, whooping cough)
•Cystic fibrosis
•Immune system deficiencies
•Chronic aspiration of food or stomach acid
•Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)
•Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
•Autoimmune or connective tissue diseases
•Primary ciliary dyskinesia
•Airway obstruction (tumor, foreign body)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed, including antibiotics, bronchodilators, and mucus-thinning agents.
•Perform airway clearance techniques daily as directed by the healthcare provider or respiratory therapist.
•Use prescribed nebulizer treatments or inhaled medications consistently.
•Stay well-hydrated to help thin mucus.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.
•Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccines.
•Avoid smoking and exposure to lung irritants.
•Seek prompt treatment for respiratory infections.
•Keep all scheduled pulmonology and PCP appointments.
•Report changes in mucus color, volume, or consistency, or worsening symptoms.

Emphysema.education:
What is Emphysema?
Emphysema is a chronic lung condition in which the air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs are damaged, making it progressively harder to breathe. The walls of the air sacs break down, creating larger air spaces instead of many small ones. This reduces the surface area of the lungs and the amount of oxygen that reaches the bloodstream. Emphysema is one of the conditions that falls under the umbrella of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Signs and Symptoms:
•Shortness of breath, especially with activity (gradually worsens over time)
•Chronic cough
•Wheezing
•Chest tightness or barrel-shaped chest
•Fatigue
•Reduced exercise tolerance
•Unintended weight loss (in advanced cases)
•Bluish discoloration of the lips or fingernails (cyanosis)

Risk Factors:
•Smoking (most significant risk factor)
•Long-term exposure to secondhand smoke
•Occupational exposure to dust, fumes, or chemical vapors
•Air pollution
•Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (a genetic condition)
•Older age
•History of childhood respiratory infections

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Stop smoking and avoid exposure to lung irritants.
•Take prescribed medications as directed, including bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and other COPD medications.
•Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
•Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
•Stay physically active as tolerated.

Thyroid Nodules.education:
What are Thyroid Nodules?
Thyroid nodules are growths or lumps that form within the thyroid gland, located in the front of the neck. Most thyroid nodules are benign (not cancerous) and do not cause symptoms. However, some nodules can become large enough to cause problems, produce excess thyroid hormone, or in rare cases, be cancerous.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Most thyroid nodules cause no symptoms and are found incidentally during a physical exam or imaging study
•A visible or palpable lump in the front of the neck
•Difficulty swallowing or a feeling of fullness in the throat
•Difficulty breathing if the nodule is large
•Hoarseness or voice changes
•Neck pain
•If the nodule produces excess thyroid hormone, symptoms of hyperthyroidism may occur (rapid heartbeat, weight loss, nervousness, tremor, increased sweating)

Risk Factors:
•Being female
•Older age
•History of radiation exposure to the head or neck
•Family history of thyroid nodules or thyroid cancer
•Iodine deficiency
•Hashimoto's thyroiditis or other thyroid conditions
•Certain genetic syndromes

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the healthcare provider's recommendations for monitoring with regular thyroid ultrasounds and blood tests.
•Take thyroid hormone medication as prescribed if indicated.
•Complete fine-needle aspiration biopsy if recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Report any changes in the size of the nodule, new difficulty swallowing or breathing, hoarseness, or neck pain.
•Discuss the need for surgery (thyroidectomy) with the healthcare provider if the nodule is large, suspicious, or causing symptoms.
•Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
•Complete recommended thyroid function laboratory tests (TSH, free T4) as ordered.

Diverticulitis.education:
What is Diverticulitis?
Diverticulitis occurs when small pouches (diverticula) that form in the walls of the colon become inflamed or infected. Diverticula are common, especially after age 40, and usually do not cause problems. When they become inflamed, the condition is called diverticulitis and can range from mild to severe.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Pain in the lower left side of the abdomen (most common)
•Fever and chills
•Nausea and vomiting
•Changes in bowel habits (constipation or diarrhea)
•Abdominal tenderness
•Bloating
•Rectal bleeding (less common)
•Urinary symptoms if the inflamed area is near the bladder

Risk Factors:
•Older age (especially over 40)
•Low-fiber diet
•Obesity
•Smoking
•Lack of physical activity
•Certain medications (NSAIDs, steroids, opioids)
•Family history of diverticular disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed antibiotics as directed during acute episodes.
•Follow the healthcare provider's dietary recommendations during and after acute episodes.
•Increase dietary fiber gradually when recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Stay well-hydrated.
•Stay physically active.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Avoid smoking.
•Complete recommended imaging and follow-up appointments.
•Report recurring abdominal pain, fever, or changes in bowel habits.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

GI Bleed.education:
What is a Gastrointestinal (GI) Bleed?
A gastrointestinal bleed is bleeding that occurs anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the rectum. GI bleeds can be acute (sudden and severe) or chronic (slow and ongoing). Upper GI bleeds originate from the esophagus, stomach, or upper small intestine. Lower GI bleeds originate from the lower small intestine, colon, or rectum.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Vomiting blood (bright red or dark, coffee-ground appearance)
•Black, tarry stools (melena)
•Bright red blood in the stool or from the rectum (hematochezia)
•Abdominal pain or cramping
•Weakness, dizziness, or lightheadedness
•Fatigue
•Pale skin
•Shortness of breath
•Rapid heartbeat
•Decreased urine output
•Fainting

Risk Factors:
•Peptic ulcer disease
•Use of NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin)
•Anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications
•Esophageal varices (often from liver disease or cirrhosis)
•Inflammatory bowel disease
•Diverticular disease
•Hemorrhoids or anal fissures
•Cancer of the GI tract
•Gastritis or esophagitis
•Heavy alcohol use
•Older age
•History of prior GI bleed

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take all prescribed medications as directed.
•Avoid NSAIDs unless approved by the healthcare provider.
•Take prescribed proton pump inhibitors or other acid-reducing medications if indicated.
•Avoid alcohol.
•Report any signs of bleeding (blood in stool, black stools, vomiting blood) immediately.
•Follow dietary recommendations from the healthcare provider.
•Complete recommended endoscopy, colonoscopy, or other diagnostic procedures.
•If on anticoagulant therapy, follow the healthcare provider's instructions carefully and complete required blood tests.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

Gallstones.education:
What are Gallstones?
Gallstones are hard, pebble-like pieces of material, usually made of cholesterol or bilirubin, that form in the gallbladder. The gallbladder is a small organ beneath the liver that stores bile, a digestive fluid. Gallstones can range in size from a grain of sand to a golf ball and may cause no symptoms or severe pain when they block the bile ducts.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Many people with gallstones have no symptoms (silent gallstones)
•Sudden, intense pain in the upper right abdomen or center of the abdomen (biliary colic)
•Pain that radiates to the right shoulder or back between the shoulder blades
•Nausea and vomiting
•Fever and chills (if infection is present)
•Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
•Clay-colored stools
•Dark urine
•Bloating or indigestion, especially after fatty meals

Risk Factors:
•Being female
•Age 40 or older
•Overweight or obesity
•Rapid weight loss or crash dieting
•Pregnancy
•Family history of gallstones
•High-fat, high-cholesterol, low-fiber diet
•Diabetes
•Certain medications (hormone therapy, cholesterol-lowering drugs)
•Native American or Hispanic descent
•Liver disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the healthcare provider's treatment recommendations.
•If surgery (cholecystectomy) is recommended, follow pre- and post-operative instructions.
•Follow dietary recommendations, especially reducing fat intake if symptomatic.
•Maintain a healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss or crash diets.
•Report recurrent abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, or changes in stool color.
•Complete recommended imaging and laboratory tests.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology, surgery, and PCP appointments.

Dysphagia.education:
What is Dysphagia?
Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing, meaning it takes more time and effort to move food or liquid from the mouth to the stomach. Dysphagia can occur at any age but is more common in older adults. It may be caused by conditions affecting the muscles, nerves, or structures involved in swallowing.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Difficulty initiating a swallow
•Food or liquid getting stuck in the throat or chest
•Pain when swallowing (odynophagia)
•Coughing or choking during or after eating or drinking
•Bringing food back up (regurgitation)
•Recurrent heartburn
•Drooling
•Hoarseness
•Sensation of a lump in the throat
•Unintended weight loss
•Recurrent pneumonia (from aspiration)
•Avoidance of certain foods due to difficulty swallowing

Risk Factors:
•Neurological conditions (stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, ALS, dementia)
•Head and neck cancer or radiation therapy
•Esophageal conditions (strictures, tumors, eosinophilic esophagitis)
•Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
•Aging and muscle weakness
•Surgery involving the head, neck, or esophagus
•Certain medications that cause dry mouth or esophageal injury

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the speech-language pathologist's and healthcare provider's swallowing recommendations.
•Follow the prescribed diet texture and liquid consistency (regular, mechanical soft, pureed, thickened liquids).
•Sit upright during meals and remain upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
•Eat slowly and take small bites and sips.
•Avoid talking while eating.
•Follow swallowing exercises as prescribed.
•Maintain adequate nutrition and hydration.
•Report new or worsening difficulty swallowing, choking, coughing during meals, or unintended weight loss.
•Keep all scheduled speech therapy, gastroenterology, and PCP appointments.

Amputation.education:
What is Amputation Aftercare?
Amputation is the surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb. Common reasons include peripheral vascular disease, diabetes-related complications, trauma, infection, or cancer. After amputation, ongoing care is essential for healing, rehabilitation, and maintaining quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms to Monitor After Amputation:
•Pain at the surgical site or phantom limb pain (sensation of pain in the limb that was removed)
•Swelling of the residual limb (stump)
•Skin changes, redness, or breakdown on the residual limb
•Wound drainage or signs of infection
•Emotional changes including grief, depression, or anxiety
•Difficulty with balance or mobility
•Phantom limb sensations (feeling as if the removed limb is still present)

Risk Factors for Amputation:
•Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) or peripheral vascular disease (PVD)
•Diabetes with poorly controlled blood sugar
•Non-healing wounds or ulcers
•Severe infection (gangrene, osteomyelitis)
•Severe trauma or crush injury
•Cancer involving the limb
•Smoking

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow wound care instructions exactly as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Keep the residual limb clean, dry, and properly bandaged or wrapped.
•Inspect the residual limb daily for redness, swelling, skin breakdown, blisters, or drainage.
•Participate in physical and occupational therapy as recommended.
•Use prescribed prosthetic devices and follow the prosthetist's fitting and care instructions.
•Perform prescribed exercises to maintain strength, flexibility, and range of motion.
•Position the residual limb as directed to prevent contractures.
•Manage pain with prescribed medications and non-drug strategies.
•Discuss phantom limb pain management with the healthcare provider.
•Address emotional and mental health needs; seek counseling or support groups.
•Manage underlying conditions (diabetes, vascular disease) to prevent complications in the remaining limb.
•Keep all scheduled surgery, rehabilitation, prosthetics, and PCP appointments.

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.education:
What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?
Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common condition that causes numbness, tingling, and weakness in the hand and wrist. It occurs when the median nerve, which runs from the forearm through a narrow passageway in the wrist called the carpal tunnel, becomes compressed or squeezed.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Numbness, tingling, or burning in the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers
•Pain in the hand, wrist, or forearm
•Weakness in the hand, especially difficulty gripping objects
•Dropping objects
•Sensation of swollen fingers even when no swelling is visible
•Symptoms often worse at night or upon waking
•Symptoms may worsen with activities that involve flexing the wrist (driving, reading, typing)
•In advanced cases, loss of sensation and muscle wasting at the base of the thumb

Risk Factors:
•Repetitive hand and wrist motions (typing, assembly line work)
•Wrist injuries or fractures
•Being female (women are more likely to develop CTS)
•Pregnancy
•Diabetes
•Rheumatoid arthritis
•Hypothyroidism
•Obesity
•Fluid retention
•Older age

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Wear a wrist splint as prescribed, especially at night.
•Take prescribed medications (anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroid injections) as directed.
•Modify activities that aggravate symptoms; take frequent breaks from repetitive hand motions.
•Perform prescribed hand and wrist stretching exercises.
•Apply cold packs to reduce swelling if recommended.
•Maintain proper wrist positioning during work and daily activities.
•Use ergonomic tools and workstation modifications.
•Discuss surgical options (carpal tunnel release) with the healthcare provider if conservative treatment does not provide relief.
•Manage underlying conditions that may contribute to CTS (diabetes, thyroid disease).
•Keep all scheduled orthopedic, neurology, and PCP appointments.

Spondylosis.education:
What is Spondylosis?
Spondylosis is a general term for age-related wear and tear (degeneration) of the spinal discs and joints. It is a form of osteoarthritis that affects the spine. Spondylosis is very common, especially in people over 60, and can occur in the cervical (neck), thoracic (mid-back), or lumbar (lower back) spine.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Stiffness and pain in the neck or back
•Pain that worsens with activity or prolonged sitting/standing
•Headaches (cervical spondylosis)
•Grinding or popping sensation with movement
•Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arms, hands, legs, or feet if nerves are compressed
•Difficulty with balance or coordination (in severe cervical cases)
•Reduced range of motion in the spine
•Muscle spasms
•Some people have no symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Aging (most significant factor)
•Prior spinal injuries
•Repetitive stress on the spine from occupation or activities
•Obesity
•Smoking
•Genetic predisposition
•Sedentary lifestyle
•Heavy lifting or manual labor

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed pain medications, anti-inflammatories, or muscle relaxants as directed.
•Participate in physical therapy to improve flexibility, strength, and posture.
•Stay physically active with low-impact exercises such as walking, swimming, or yoga.
•Maintain proper posture and body mechanics.
•Use ergonomic supports when sitting or sleeping.
•Apply heat or cold therapy as recommended.
•Maintain a healthy weight to reduce stress on the spine.
•Stop smoking.
•Consider epidural steroid injections or surgical options if recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Keep all scheduled orthopedic, neurosurgery, and PCP appointments.

Wound Care.education:
What is Wound Care?
Wound care involves the management and treatment of wounds to promote healing and prevent complications such as infection. Wounds can include surgical incisions, pressure injuries (bedsores), diabetic ulcers, venous or arterial ulcers, traumatic wounds, and burns. Proper wound care is essential for preventing infection and promoting tissue repair.

Signs and Symptoms to Monitor:
•Redness, warmth, or swelling around the wound
•Increased pain or tenderness at the wound site
•Drainage from the wound (clear, yellow, green, or foul-smelling)
•Wound edges that are separating or not closing
•Darkening or discoloration of the wound or surrounding skin
•Fever or chills
•Slow or stalled healing progress
•Numbness around the wound

Risk Factors for Poor Wound Healing:
•Diabetes with poorly controlled blood sugar
•Peripheral vascular disease or poor circulation
•Obesity
•Malnutrition or protein deficiency
•Smoking
•Immunosuppression (medications, medical conditions)
•Older age
•Prolonged immobility or pressure on the skin
•Chronic kidney disease
•Certain medications (corticosteroids, anticoagulants)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow wound care instructions exactly as directed by the healthcare provider or wound care specialist.
•Keep the wound clean using prescribed cleansing solutions.
•Change dressings at the recommended frequency using the prescribed materials.
•Wash hands thoroughly before and after wound care.
•Monitor the wound daily for signs of infection or changes.
•Keep the wound protected and avoid unnecessary touching.

Atopic Dermatitis.education:
What is Atopic Dermatitis?
Atopic dermatitis, commonly known as eczema, is a chronic skin condition that causes dry, itchy, and inflamed skin. It is the most common type of eczema and often begins in childhood but can occur at any age. Atopic dermatitis tends to flare up periodically and then subside.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Dry, cracked skin
•Itching, which may be severe, especially at night
•Red to brownish-gray patches on the skin
•Small, raised bumps that may leak fluid when scratched
•Thickened, scaly skin from repeated scratching (lichenification)
•Raw, sensitive, or swollen skin from scratching
•Common locations: hands, feet, ankles, wrists, neck, upper chest, eyelids, inside the bend of elbows and knees, and in infants, the face and scalp

Risk Factors:
•Family history of eczema, allergies, hay fever, or asthma
•Personal history of allergies or asthma
•Childhood onset (most common)
•Living in dry or cold climates
•Living in urban areas
•Exposure to environmental irritants

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Apply prescribed moisturizers (emollients) liberally and frequently, especially after bathing.
•Use prescribed topical medications (corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, PDE4 inhibitors) as directed.
•Take prescribed oral or injectable medications (immunomodulators, biologics) if indicated.
•Bathe in lukewarm water for short periods and pat skin dry gently.
•Avoid known triggers (harsh soaps, fragrances, certain fabrics, allergens, stress, extreme temperatures).
•Use mild, fragrance-free soaps, detergents, and skin care products.
•Wear soft, breathable clothing (cotton).
•Keep fingernails trimmed to reduce skin damage from scratching.
•Use wet wrap therapy if recommended by the healthcare provider.
•Manage stress, which can trigger flares.
•Keep all scheduled dermatology and PCP appointments.

Basal Cell Carcinoma.education:
What is Basal Cell Carcinoma?
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer. It arises from the basal cells, which are found in the deepest layer of the outer skin (epidermis). BCC typically grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body, but it can cause significant local damage if not treated.

Signs and Symptoms:
•A pearly or waxy bump on the face, ears, or neck
•A flat, flesh-colored or brown scar-like lesion on the chest or back
•A sore that bleeds, oozes, crusts, and does not heal, or heals and returns
•A pink growth with a slightly raised, rolled border and a crusted center
•A shiny bump or nodule that is translucent and may have visible blood vessels
•An area that looks like a scar without a known injury

Risk Factors:
•Chronic or excessive sun exposure (UV radiation)
•History of sunburns, especially blistering sunburns
•Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
•Older age
•Male sex
•History of prior skin cancer
•Use of tanning beds
•Exposure to radiation therapy
•Immunosuppression
•Exposure to arsenic
•Certain genetic conditions (basal cell nevus syndrome)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the dermatologist's treatment plan (surgical excision, Mohs surgery, cryotherapy, topical treatments, or other therapies).
•Attend regular follow-up skin examinations as recommended.
•Perform monthly skin self-examinations.
•Protect skin from UV exposure: use broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher), wear protective clothing, seek shade, and avoid peak sun hours.
•Avoid tanning beds.
•Report any new, changing, or non-healing skin lesions promptly.
•Keep all scheduled dermatology and PCP appointments.

Medication Induced Coagulopathy.education:
What is Medication Induced Coagulopathy?
Medication induced coagulopathy is a condition in which medications, most commonly anticoagulants (blood thinners) or antiplatelet agents, interfere with the blood's normal ability to clot. While these medications are prescribed to prevent harmful blood clots, they can increase the risk of bleeding. Careful monitoring and management are essential to balance the benefits of the medication with the risk of bleeding.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Easy bruising or bruising that is larger than expected
•Prolonged bleeding from cuts or wounds
•Nosebleeds that are frequent or difficult to stop
•Bleeding gums
•Blood in the urine (pink, red, or cola-colored)
•Blood in the stool (bright red or black, tarry stools)
•Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding
•Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
•Unexplained or excessive bleeding after dental work, surgery, or minor procedures
•Coughing up blood
•Severe headache, dizziness, or weakness (possible internal bleeding)

Risk Factors:
•Use of anticoagulant medications (warfarin, heparin, enoxaparin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran)
•Use of antiplatelet medications (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel)
•Older age
•Kidney or liver disease affecting drug metabolism
•Drug interactions (antibiotics, antifungals, NSAIDs, herbal supplements)
•Frequent falls
•History of GI bleeding or peptic ulcer disease
•Uncontrolled high blood pressure
•Low body weight
•Excessive alcohol use

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications exactly as prescribed at the same time each day.
•Do not stop, skip, or double doses without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Complete all required blood tests (INR/PT for warfarin; CBC as indicated) on schedule.
•Inform all healthcare providers, dentists, and pharmacists that you are taking blood thinners.
•Wear medical identification indicating anticoagulant use.
•Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) unless approved by the healthcare provider.
•Discuss all new medications, supplements, vitamins, and herbal products with the healthcare provider before starting them.
•Use a soft-bristled toothbrush and electric razor to reduce injury risk.
•Avoid activities with a high risk of injury or falls.
•Apply direct pressure to cuts and hold for several minutes until bleeding stops.
•If on warfarin, maintain consistent vitamin K intake (do not drastically change intake of green leafy vegetables).
•Report any signs of unusual bleeding promptly.
•Keep all scheduled PCP, hematology, and anticoagulation clinic appointments.

Consistent Diet for Anticoagulant Management:
If taking warfarin, maintaining a consistent daily intake of vitamin K is essential for stable anticoagulation. Vitamin K is found in green leafy vegetables (kale, spinach, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, collard greens). The goal is not to eliminate these foods but to eat a consistent amount each day so that the warfarin dose can be adjusted accordingly. Sudden large changes in vitamin K intake can cause the INR to fluctuate, increasing the risk of bleeding or clotting. For newer anticoagulants (DOACs), vitamin K consistency is not required, but a balanced diet and limited alcohol intake are still recommended.
diet.overview: Vitamin K and Anticoagulant Diet: For patients on warfarin, maintaining a consistent daily intake of vitamin K is essential — the goal is not to eliminate vitamin K-rich foods but to eat a consistent amount each day so the medication dose can be calibrated accordingly. Sudden increases or decreases in vitamin K intake can cause dangerous fluctuations in blood clotting. For patients on newer anticoagulants (DOACs), dietary restrictions are generally less strict, but alcohol should still be limited.

Addison's Disease.education:
What is Addison's Disease?
Addison's disease, also known as primary adrenal insufficiency, is a condition in which the adrenal glands do not produce enough of certain hormones, particularly cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol helps the body respond to stress, maintain blood pressure, regulate metabolism, and reduce inflammation. Aldosterone helps regulate sodium and potassium levels. Addison's disease can be life-threatening if not treated.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Extreme fatigue and weakness
•Unintended weight loss and decreased appetite
•Darkening of the skin (hyperpigmentation), especially in skin folds, scars, and gums
•Low blood pressure, including dizziness or fainting when standing
•Salt cravings
•Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
•Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain
•Muscle or joint pain
•Irritability or depression
•Body hair loss or sexual dysfunction (in women)

Adrenal Crisis (Emergency):
•Severe weakness
•Severe pain in the lower back, abdomen, or legs
•Severe nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea leading to dehydration
•Low blood pressure and loss of consciousness
•High potassium and low sodium levels

Risk Factors:
•Autoimmune disorders (most common cause)
•Tuberculosis
•Other infections affecting the adrenal glands
•Bleeding into the adrenal glands
•Cancer that has spread to the adrenal glands
•Surgical removal of the adrenal glands
•Long-term use of corticosteroids followed by sudden discontinuation
•Family history of autoimmune conditions

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed hormone replacement medications (hydrocortisone, prednisone, or fludrocortisone) exactly as directed.
•Never skip or stop taking medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
•Learn to adjust medication doses during illness, injury, or surgery (stress dosing) as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Carry a medical alert identification card and wear medical alert jewelry.
•Carry an emergency injectable corticosteroid kit and know how to use it.
•Maintain adequate sodium intake as recommended.
•Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
•Inform all healthcare providers, dentists, and emergency personnel about the diagnosis.
•Report signs of adrenal crisis immediately.
•Receive recommended vaccinations.

Overactive Bladder.education:
What is Overactive Bladder (OAB)?
Overactive bladder is a condition characterized by a sudden, frequent, and difficult-to-control urge to urinate. It may result in the involuntary loss of urine (urge incontinence). OAB can significantly affect quality of life but is treatable through behavioral strategies, medications, and other interventions.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Urinary urgency — a sudden, strong need to urinate that is difficult to control
•Frequent urination — needing to urinate more than eight times in 24 hours
•Urge incontinence — involuntary loss of urine immediately following an urgent need to urinate
•Nocturia — waking two or more times during the night to urinate

Risk Factors:
•Older age
•Menopause and estrogen deficiency
•Enlarged prostate (BPH) in men
•Neurological conditions (stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury)
•Diabetes
•Urinary tract infections
•Pelvic surgery or radiation
•Obesity
•Excessive caffeine or alcohol intake
•Certain medications (diuretics)
•Pregnancy and childbirth
•Weakened pelvic floor muscles

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Practice bladder retraining techniques as directed by the healthcare provider.
•Perform pelvic floor muscle exercises (Kegel exercises) regularly.
•Maintain a bladder diary to track urination patterns, fluid intake, and episodes of urgency or leakage.
•Limit or avoid caffeine and alcohol, which can irritate the bladder.
•Manage fluid intake — drink adequate but not excessive amounts, and limit fluids in the evening.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Manage constipation, which can worsen OAB symptoms.
•Take prescribed medications (anticholinergics such as oxybutynin, or beta-3 agonists such as mirabegron) as directed.
•Discuss advanced treatment options (Botox injections, nerve stimulation, surgery) with the healthcare provider if needed.
•Keep all scheduled urology, urogynecology, and PCP appointments.

Bladder Retraining and Kegel.education:
What is Bladder Retraining and Kegel Exercise?
Bladder retraining and Kegel exercises are behavioral therapies used to improve bladder control and reduce urinary incontinence. They are often recommended for people with overactive bladder, urge incontinence, or stress incontinence.

Bladder Retraining Instructions:
•Empty your bladder as soon as you get up in the morning. This starts your retraining schedule.
•Go to the bathroom at the specific times you and your healthcare provider have discussed. Wait until your next scheduled time before urinating again.
•Be sure to empty your bladder at each scheduled time, even if you feel no urge to urinate.
•When you have accomplished your initial goal, gradually increase the time between emptying your bladder by 15-minute intervals.
•Try to increase your interval each week.
•If you feel the urge to urinate before your scheduled time, use relaxation techniques: stop and stand still or sit down, take slow deep breaths, squeeze your pelvic floor muscles, and wait until the urge passes before walking slowly to the bathroom.
•It should take between 6 to 12 weeks to accomplish your goal.

Kegel Exercise Instructions:
•To do a Kegel exercise, squeeze the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or prevent passing gas.
•Do not tighten the muscles of your abdomen, buttocks, or thighs. Focus only on the pelvic floor muscles.
•To complete one set, squeeze your pelvic floor muscles for a slow count of three, then relax the muscles completely for a slow count of three.
•Do not push the muscles outward during the relaxation phase.
•Repeat 10 times to complete one set (10 squeezes equal one set).
•Perform three sets each day (morning, afternoon, and evening).
•As your muscle strength improves, increase the squeeze and relaxation count to five seconds each.
•Be consistent — results require regular, daily exercise over several weeks.

Signs and Symptoms That May Indicate the Need for Bladder Retraining:
•Frequent urination (more than eight times in 24 hours)
•Sudden, strong urges to urinate
•Urge incontinence (leaking urine before reaching the bathroom)
•Nocturia (waking at night to urinate)
•Stress incontinence (leaking urine with coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercise)

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Follow the bladder retraining schedule consistently.
•Perform Kegel exercises daily as recommended.
•Keep a bladder diary to track progress.
•Report improvements or difficulties to the healthcare provider.
•Combine bladder retraining and Kegel exercises with other treatments as directed.
•Be patient — improvement typically takes 6 to 12 weeks of consistent practice.
•Keep all scheduled urology, urogynecology, or PCP appointments.

GERD.education:
What is GERD?
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition in which stomach acid frequently flows back into the esophagus (the tube connecting the mouth to the stomach). This backwash of acid (acid reflux) can irritate and damage the lining of the esophagus over time.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Heartburn — a burning sensation in the chest, usually after eating, that may worsen when lying down
•Acid or food coming back into the mouth (regurgitation)
•Sour or bitter taste in the mouth
•Difficulty swallowing
•Chronic cough
•Hoarseness or sore throat
•Feeling like there is a lump in the throat
•Chest pain (non-cardiac)
•Symptoms that worsen after eating or when lying down
•Worsening of asthma symptoms

Risk Factors:
•Obesity or overweight
•Hiatal hernia
•Pregnancy
•Smoking
•Eating large meals or eating late at night
•Certain foods (fatty, fried, spicy, acidic)
•Certain beverages (coffee, alcohol, carbonated drinks)
•Certain medications (aspirin, NSAIDs, some blood pressure medications)
•Connective tissue disorders such as scleroderma
•Delayed stomach emptying

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed (antacids, H2 blockers such as famotidine, or proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole).
•Eat smaller, more frequent meals.
•Avoid eating 2-3 hours before bedtime.
•Elevate the head of the bed 6-8 inches if nighttime symptoms occur.
•Maintain a healthy weight.
•Avoid tight-fitting clothing around the waist.
•Stop smoking.
•Limit alcohol intake.
•Identify and avoid personal trigger foods.
•Stay hydrated.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques and regular exercise.
•Report persistent or worsening symptoms, difficulty swallowing, or unintended weight loss.
•Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

Migraine.education:
What is Migraine?
Migraine is a neurological condition that causes recurring episodes of moderate to severe headache, often accompanied by other symptoms affecting the nervous system and body. Migraine is more than just a headache — it can be debilitating and may interfere with daily activities at home, work, and school. Untreated migraine attacks typically last between 4 and 72 hours.

Signs and Symptoms:
•Intense, throbbing, or pulsing headache, often on one side of the head but sometimes on both sides
•Nausea and vomiting
•Sensitivity to light, sound, or smells
•Dizziness or lightheadedness
•Fatigue or weakness
•Visual disturbances (aura), such as flashing lights, zigzag lines, or blind spots
•Numbness or tingling, usually in the face or hands (aura)
•Difficulty concentrating or thinking clearly (brain fog)
•Mood changes, irritability, or depression before or after an attack
•Neck stiffness
•Food cravings or loss of appetite before an attack
•Yawning excessively before an attack (prodromal phase)

Risk Factors:
•Family history of migraine (strong genetic component)
•Being female (women are three times more likely than men to experience migraine)
•Hormonal changes (menstruation, pregnancy, menopause, oral contraceptive use)
•Age (most commonly begins in teens to early twenties)
•Stress
•Sleep disturbances (too much or too little sleep, irregular sleep schedule)
•Certain foods and beverages (alcohol, aged cheeses, chocolate, caffeine, processed foods, foods containing MSG or nitrates)
•Environmental factors (bright or flickering lights, strong smells, loud sounds, weather changes)
•Dehydration
•Skipping meals
•Other medical conditions (depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, sleep disorders, epilepsy)
•Tobacco use

Treatment and Self-Management:
•Take prescribed medications as directed. Migraine medications may include acute treatments (triptans, NSAIDs, anti-nausea medications, gepants) and preventive treatments (beta-blockers, anticonvulsants, antidepressants, CGRP monoclonal antibodies, or Botox injections).
•Take acute migraine medication at the first sign of an attack for best effectiveness.
•Avoid overusing acute pain medications, which can lead to medication-overuse headache (rebound headache).
•Keep a headache diary or journal to track frequency, duration, triggers, symptoms, and response to treatment.
•Identify and avoid personal migraine triggers.
•Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
•Stay well-hydrated and do not skip meals.
•Manage stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, biofeedback, or cognitive behavioral therapy.
•Stay physically active with regular, moderate exercise as tolerated.
•Rest in a quiet, dark room during an attack.
•Apply cold packs to the forehead or neck if helpful.
•Discuss preventive medication options with the healthcare provider if migraines occur frequently (4 or more days per month), are severe, or significantly interfere with daily life.
•Keep all scheduled neurology and PCP appointments.

diet.overview: Migraine Diet: Certain foods and dietary habits can trigger or worsen migraine attacks. Keeping a food diary can help identify personal dietary triggers. Common food triggers include aged cheeses, alcohol (especially red wine), chocolate, caffeine (both excess and withdrawal), processed meats containing nitrates, foods with MSG, and artificial sweeteners. Maintaining regular meal times, staying well-hydrated, and avoiding known personal triggers are key dietary strategies for migraine management.
eat_more: Magnesium-rich foods such as spinach, almonds, cashews, pumpkin seeds, and black beans
Foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids such as salmon, sardines, and flaxseed
Foods rich in riboflavin (vitamin B2) such as eggs, lean meats, and fortified cereals
Adequate water throughout the day (at least 6-8 glasses)
limit: Caffeine to a consistent, moderate amount (sudden changes in caffeine intake can trigger migraine)
Alcohol, especially red wine and beer
Aged cheeses (cheddar, blue cheese, parmesan, brie)
Processed and cured meats (hot dogs, bacon, deli meats) containing nitrates or nitrites
Chocolate, if identified as a personal trigger
avoid: Skipping meals or fasting, which can trigger migraine
Sudden changes in caffeine intake (either significant increase or abrupt withdrawal)
Foods identified as personal migraine triggers
guidelines: Keep a food diary to identify personal dietary triggers
Eat regular meals at consistent times throughout the day
Stay well-hydrated — dehydration is a common migraine trigger
Limit but do not abruptly stop caffeine if it is a regular part of your diet
Discuss magnesium, riboflavin, or CoQ10 supplementation with the healthcare provider
Follow any individualized dietary recommendations from the healthcare provider

call_911: Sudden, severe headache that is the worst headache of your life (thunderclap headache)
Headache accompanied by fever, stiff neck, confusion, seizure, double vision, weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking
Headache after a head injury
Headache with loss of consciousness
Headache that is progressively worsening and unlike any previous headache
New headache with sudden vision loss
Severe headache with signs of stroke (facial drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty)
call_provider: Migraines that are increasing in frequency or severity
New headache pattern or change in the character of usual headaches
Migraines not responding to current treatment
Need for acute migraine medication more than 2-3 times per week
Migraines significantly interfering with work, school, or daily activities
New or worsening aura symptoms
Side effects from migraine medications
Migraine with new neurological symptoms not previously experienced
Waking from sleep due to headache
Persistent nausea or vomiting with migraine that prevents keeping medications or fluids down
